questions.q: For a service with a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day window, what is its error budget?
options: The remaining 0.1%, roughly 43 minutes of allowed unavailability in that window
A fixed dollar amount set by finance each quarter
Exactly 99.9% of the window, i.e. almost the entire 30 days
There is no error budget unless the SLO is below 99%
questions.explain: Error budget is 1 - SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days, the remaining 0.1% works out to roughly 43 minutes of allowed unavailability, spent by SLI violations.

questions.q: According to the Google SRE book's framing in this lesson, what is the real purpose of an error budget?
options: It exists purely for historical reporting, with no bearing on current decisions
It serves as a negotiated agreement between product development and SRE about acceptable risk, decided in advance rather than argued over during an incident
It determines employee bonuses at the end of the fiscal year
It replaces the need for SLIs and SLOs entirely
questions.explain: The error budget turns an abstract reliability-versus-velocity tradeoff into an objective number both product and SRE already agreed to respect ahead of time, rather than a fresh fight during every incident.

questions.q: What is the well-documented, enforced consequence when a team's error budget policy says the budget is fully exhausted?
options: Nothing changes operationally; it is only a dashboard indicator
The team stops shipping new features and redirects engineering capacity to reliability work until the budget recovers
The service is immediately decommissioned
The SLO is automatically lowered so the budget resets to full
questions.explain: A real error budget policy enforces a feature freeze once the budget is exhausted — the team's capacity shifts entirely to reliability work, with SRE holding the authority to say no to further launches.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'fast burn' from a 'slow burn' of an error budget, per this lesson?
options: Fast burn only applies to databases, slow burn only applies to APIs
They are identical; burn rate has no effect on the response
A fast burn consumes the budget in hours due to an active outage and triggers immediate paging; a slow burn consumes it gradually over days and triggers a scheduled policy review instead
A slow burn means the SLO was set too high and must be abandoned
questions.explain: Alerting on burn rate lets an organization tell these two situations apart: fast burn means 'stop the bleeding now' via incident response, slow burn means a scheduled review of systemic reliability debt.

questions.q: Why does an error budget policy matter more at the scale of hundreds of services than at the scale of one?
options: It doesn't — the policy is only useful for a single service
It lets the organization apply the same feature-freeze decision consistently and fairly across many teams, without a VP personally adjudicating every case
Error budgets become optional once there are more than ten services
At scale, error budgets are calculated in dollars instead of percentages
questions.explain: At one service, an exhausted budget is a conversation between two people. Across hundreds of services, the written policy is what lets that same decision happen consistently everywhere, functioning as real governance.
